awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of an In-Ear Blood Pressure Monitoring System for Future Wearable Health Technologies
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project is based on the development of a miniaturized in-ear blood pressure monitoring device. Current cuff-based blood pressure monitoring devices require proper positioning and although user training is inconvenient, it is required to avoid user error. Wearable blood pressure monitors (wrist, armband, and finger) are susceptible to inaccurate readings due to position and motion sensitivity. Wearable devices must be positioned at heart level for an accurate reading. In addition, most blood pressure devices lack automatic data logging and remote monitoring capability. This technology is a wearable form factor that may provide a stable and reliable location for blood pressure monitoring. The device is a hearing-aid-like earpiece that is designed for accurate and frequent blood pressure monitoring. This solution may be well suited for patients with hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and eclampsia. Such patients need frequent blood pressure monitoring, typically several times per day. This technology may offer a less disruptive alternative to cuff-based measurements and provide a more accurate way to monitor blood pressure frequently, which is important for improving health outcomes for patients with hypertension and related diseases.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of a medical device to measure blood pressure. The ear is a preferred site for accurate blood pressure measurements due to its dense vascular structure, fewer motion artifacts, and fixed distance from the heart (as compared with cuff-based and other wearable blood pressure monitoring devices). This technology uses a light-based pulse sensor inserted gently into the ear canal, coupled with a digital air pump for precise control, and a blood pressure estimation algorithm. The device’s sensor provides accurate systolic and diastolic blood pressure values and pulse rate by gradually inflating in the ear canal, without obstructing blood flow. The technology is based on a key finding that the pulse waveform can be detected through a sensing mechanism, and blood pressure can be identified through an algorithm without completely blocking the artery. In addition, the device may provide feedback to a mobile application, enabling users to track their blood pressure trends and receive artificial intelligence (AI)-generated insights for improved health management. The goal is to provide a more accurate and less disruptive solution for patients suffering from hypertension and related diseases that require frequent blood pressure monitoring.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
During the NSF I-Corps program, our team investigated the commercial viability of the eBP device designed to support frequent, continuous BP monitoring outside of clinical settings. Our goal was to validate real market need and problem-solution fit before committing further engineering resources to the device.

Over the duration of the program, the team conducted more than 80 informal stakeholder discussions and interviews across six industry conferences (MedCon 2025, 10x2025: Humanizing MedTech, MedTech MVP, the JP Morgan Healthcare Conference, MD&M West Expo 2026, and NEXUS 2026), engaging clinicians, patients, regulatory consultants, manufacturing partners, reimbursement experts, and investors. Through these extensive conversations with clinicians, regulatory experts, manufacturing partners, and patients, we challenged our initial assumptions. Rather than targeting a broad, generalized "hypertension" market, our findings revealed that the highest urgency, clearest clinical need, and most straightforward reimbursement pathways exist within the pregnancy hypertension space (specifically addressing preeclampsia and gestational hypertension). Consequently, we refined our business framework to establish pregnancy-induced hypertension as our primary beachhead market, with a particular focus on the underserved two-week postpartum window. Also, we identified chronic kidney disease and cardiovascular patients as secondary segments, and contract research organizations (CROs) as an institutional segment for non-invasive BP monitoring in clinical trials.

Key Outcomes:
  • Market Refinement: The team shifted away from a direct-to-consumer marketing approach. Customer discovery proved that clinical influencers and prescribers (such as OB/GYNs, nephrologists, and cardiologists) serve as the vital gatekeepers necessary to drive actual patient adoption and device trust.
  • Regulatory & Engineering Re-alignment: Conversations with regulatory consultants confirmed that a combination hardware-software device must integrate risk management, data privacy, and FDA 510(k) Class II compliance pathways directly into the MVP architecture from day one. We have engaged an FDA consultant to finalize predicate device analysis and structure our formal regulatory submission timeline.
  • Strategic Partnerships: The team successfully established guidance on manufacturing quality-assurance protocols and contract manufacturing pipelines. We have mapped out explicit pre-launch development partnerships and are engaging 2–3 contract manufacturing firms alongside clinical design advisors at the University of Colorado.
  • Funding Strategy: We opened direct conversations with ARPA-H program managers on non-dilutive capital, which we are pursuing alongside traditional investor relationships as our next-stage funding strategy.


Broader Impacts:
This project sharpened our team's entrepreneurial mindset. Instead of classroom instruction, we practiced hands-on, hypothesis-driven customer discovery. Over six conferences and multiple geographies, we engaged with clinicians, regulators, manufacturers, and investors. Through these interactions, we strengthened our ability to test assumptions against real evidence. We also learned to translate clinical and technical findings into business decisions. Along the way, we incorporated mentor feedback into how we framed our conclusions. Looking ahead, commercialization of the eBP device has the potential to improve outcomes for patients who need continuous BP monitoring, especially during high-risk periods such as pregnancy and the postpartum window. In these moments, timely detection of dangerous blood pressure levels can reduce the risk of hospitalization, stroke, and other severe complications.
